summary: Specifies a way for DNS resolvers to publish information about themselves, so DNS clients can learn their capabilities. How clients use that information is out of scope.

plainLanguage.summary: A resolver can now post a short profile about what it can do, so users can decide whether to pick it.

questions: what is the dns resinfo record
how does a client learn resolver capabilities
what is the exterr key in dns
subtitle: A new DNS record type, RESINFO, lets a resolver describe its own features to the clients that use it.

tldr.problem: DNS clients can discover encrypted resolvers, but cannot ask those resolvers about their capabilities, such as privacy features or filtering, when choosing between them.
tldr.mechanism: A client queries the RESINFO resource record type and gets key/value pairs in TXT-style format. The initial keys are qnamemin, exterr and infourl.
tldr.outcome: Clients get a more reliable way to learn what a resolver does. How they use it, and how to select a resolver, is deliberately out of scope.

today: RFC 9606 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines only how resolver information is published and retrieved, and leaves resolver selection to clients.

sections.title: Why Resolvers Need to Describe Themselves
sections.content:
Historically, DNS clients talked to recursive resolvers without needing to know what features those resolvers supported. Now resolvers expose features that affect the service, such as privacy preservation, filtering and transparent behavior. Clients can already discover and authenticate encrypted resolvers using DNR (RFC 9463) and DDR (RFC 9462), but cannot ask those resolvers what they can do.

RFC 9606 fills that gap with a new resource record type. Examples of how a client might use the information: prefer resolvers that enable QNAME minimisation (RFC 9156), pick a resolver that filters domains and reports it with the Blocked (15) Extended DNS Error (RFC 8914), or avoid one that uses Forged Answer (4). The RFC does not define selection procedures or policies. The information is scoped to properties used to infer privacy and transparency policies, and is not intended for end-user consumption.
sections.plainLanguage: Some helpers at the phone book desk keep your questions private and some do not. This gives each helper a way to say what they do, so you can pick one you trust.

sections.title: Retrieving Resolver Information
sections.content:
A client that wants resolver information queries the new RESINFO RR type. If the resolver understands it, the RRset MUST have exactly one record, and clients MUST silently ignore invalid records. RESINFO is a property of the resolver and is not subject to recursive resolution.

The QNAME is normally the Authentication Domain Name (ADN) the client used to authenticate the resolver, as in DNR. If the resolver was discovered through the special-use domain resolver.arpa (RFC 9462), the QNAME is resolver.arpa. In that case the resolver might not support RESINFO and might pass the query upstream, so a positive answer could come from an attacker.

The client MUST set the Recursion Desired (RD) bit to 0 and MUST discard the response if the AA flag is 0. Resolvers sharing an ADN or anycast address SHOULD expose a consistent RESINFO.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the helper directly, 'tell me about yourself,' and not 'go ask someone else.' If the answer did not come straight from that helper, you throw it away.

sections.title: Record Format
sections.content:
The RESINFO record uses the same format as DNS TXT records, whose rules come from RFC 1035 and are elaborated in DNS-SD (RFC 6763), including the advice to keep TXT records small. Like DNS-SD, it carries information as key/value pairs, encoded with the rules of Section 6.3 of RFC 6763, and follows the key rules of its Section 6.4.

A key with no = is a boolean attribute, simply present with no value. Clients MUST silently ignore unknown keys, which makes it easy to add keys later. Keys MUST either be in the IANA registry or begin with temp- for local use only.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile card is a list of short labels, like 'likes: privacy'. If you see a label you do not know, you just skip it.

sections.title: The Initial Keys
sections.content:
Three keys are defined, all optional.

  • qnamemin: present means the resolver is configured to minimise the privacy-sensitive data it sends to an authoritative name server (QNAME minimisation, RFC 9156). It has no value.
  • exterr: lists the Extended DNS Error codes (RFC 8914) the resolver can return. A value can be one code or a range joined by a hyphen, and non-contiguous values are comma-separated. Examples of returned codes are Blocked (15), Censored (16) and Filtered (17). If a client sees an EDE not listed, it can query again, and if a mismatch persists it can treat the information as inaccurate and discard it.
  • infourl: a URL pointing to unstructured information for troubleshooting, such as supported DoH APIs or how to report a problem. The scheme MUST be https or the URL is invalid and ignored, and the server MUST only support the content-type text/html. It is diagnostic information for IT staff only, since it could be misleading.
sections.plainLanguage: The card has three lines: 'I keep your questions private,' 'here are the kinds of error messages I can give,' and 'here is a web page if you need help.'

sections.title: An Example
sections.content: The RFC shows one published record. A client that found the ADN resolver.example.net through DNR queries RESINFO for it and learns three things: the resolver enables QNAME minimisation; it can return Blocked (15), Censored (16) and Filtered (17) EDEs; and more information is at https://resolver.example.com/guide.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading the example card tells you the helper keeps questions private, can explain why something was blocked, and has a help page.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clients MUST use one of two measures to prevent response forgery: an authenticated secure connection to the resolver, or local DNSSEC validation to verify the resolver information. Only the first applies to queries for resolver.arpa.

An encrypted resolver can still return incorrect information. If the client cannot validate the attributes it will use for selection or display, it should process them only when the resolver has sufficient reputation under local policy (user configuration, administrative configuration, or a built-in list of reputable resolvers). That limits the harm a malicious resolver can do with false claims.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper could lie on its profile card. So you should only believe the card if you reached the helper safely, or if you already trust that helper.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the RESINFO RR type with value 261 and meaning 'Resolver Information as Key/Value Pairs'. It also created a registry called 'DNS Resolver Information Keys', with the Specification Required policy and initial entries qnamemin, exterr and infourl. Names beginning with temp- are never registered, so anyone can use them freely.

Designated experts should consider the security implications of new keys and avoid duplicates. Requests are evaluated within a two-week review period, and the experts either approve or deny them.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now an official list of allowed labels for the profile card, and a number reserved for this kind of record.
